cases.input:
Got this bug bounty submission in on the Meridian Freight customer portal. Can you tell me the exact thing to run to check if it's real?

---
Title: IDOR on invoice download exposes other customers' invoices
Severity: High
Submitted by: researcher handle quietloop99

Description:
The invoice download endpoint takes a numeric invoice id and does not check that the requesting account owns that invoice. By incrementing the id, any authenticated customer can pull any other customer's invoice PDF, which includes billing address and the last four digits of the card on file.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Log in as any customer account on https://portal.meridianfreight.example.com
2. Note your own invoice id in the URL when you view your most recent invoice, e.g. invoice id 48213
3. Replace the id with a lower number, e.g. 48190, while keeping your own session cookie
4. The PDF for a different customer's invoice downloads successfully

Request observed in the browser network tab:
GET /api/invoices/48190/download HTTP/1.1
Host: portal.meridianfreight.example.com
Cookie: session=the logged-in customer's own session cookie

Impact: any customer can enumerate and download every other customer's invoices and partial card data by walking the id space.
cases.expects: The answer is the single runnable command, preceded by the command name, that validates the IDOR by swapping the invoice id while keeping the tester's own session cookie, with no extra prose, hedging or write-up around it.

cases.input:
Run extract_poc on this one:

Subject: Internal SSRF via webhook URL validation bypass on Lantern Analytics

The "webhook test" feature on the integrations settings page accepts a destination URL and fires a POST to it so the customer can confirm their endpoint is reachable. The server only blocks hostnames that resolve to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 directly, but a DNS name that first resolves to a public IP and then, via a second lookup, resolves to the internal metadata address passes the check, because the validator and the actual outbound fetch resolve the hostname separately (TOCTOU on DNS).

To prove it:
- Register a DNS name at a domain you control that you can flip between answers, e.g. rebind.example.net
- Point it first at 203.0.113.9 (a public IP you also control) so it passes the initial validation request
- Immediately flip the DNS answer to 169.254.169.254 before the server's outbound fetch happens
- Submit the webhook test with destination http://rebind.example.net/latest/meta-data/ and the target app
- Watch the webhook delivery log on your own listener at 203.0.113.9 (which never gets hit) and instead see the response body in the app's "last webhook result" field contain cloud metadata contents, proving the second request landed on the internal address

This was tested against the staging tenant only.
cases.expects: The answer is the runnable command (or exact sequence of commands) that fires the webhook test against the DNS-rebinding domain to the metadata address, stated as a command preceded by its name, not a restatement of the vulnerability narrative.

cases.input:
triage this, it's a mess, the researcher pasted their whole scratch notes:

ok so poked around api.northlake-books.example for a few hours. first thing, rate limiting on /api/login seems off, tried like 40 bad passwords in a row on test@example.com and never got blocked, might be worth someone checking that properly later, didn't finish.

then found something more interesting on the review endpoint. you can edit someone else's book review if you know the review id. the edit form is at /reviews/edit?id=991 and if you change the id in that URL to one that isn't yours (I used 990, which belonged to another test account I made, reviewer2@example.com) and submit the edit form, it saves fine even though 990 wasn't mine. no auth check on ownership before the save. here's the raw request I captured when I did it:

PUT /api/reviews/990 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.northlake-books.example
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=cookie belonging to my first test account

{"rating":1,"text":"edited by wrong account to prove the bug"}

also noticed the search endpoint throws a full stack trace with file paths when you send a weird unicode string but idk if that's even a real finding, probably not worth much. anyway the review edit thing is the one I'd actually report, the rest is just stuff I noticed along the way and didn't fully run down.
cases.expects: The answer isolates the one finding the researcher actually reproduced, the unauthorized review edit, and returns its exact validating command (the captured PUT request as a runnable curl, or equivalent), leaving out the unconfirmed rate-limit and stack-trace observations since the pattern extracts the proof-of-concept for the vulnerability, not a triage of every note.
